strengths: Addresses a timely and highly realistic challenge in personalized federated learning (PFL): joint model architecture heterogeneity and continual data/task distribution shifts in multi-modal LLMs.

The proposed PQ-LoRA is an elegant parameter-efficient adapter design that decouples low-rank parameter sharing from hidden dimension size and depth differences via block-wise relative-depth placement and pre-alignment.

SIMA provides an effective similarity-aware aggregation mechanism using exponentially decayed gradients from a frozen auxiliary model, successfully tackling parameter interference under dynamic distribution shifts.

DRAKE is a well-designed, comprehensive benchmark spanning 40 distinct multimodal tasks across diverse domains and formats, significantly advancing realistic PFL evaluation beyond synthetic label-skew splits.

Extensive experimental evaluation across multimodal (DRAKE, HFLB) and NLP (FedAya, FedLLM) setups, supported by detailed ablation studies, CKA representations analysis, and computational complexity profiling.
weaknesses: The experimental federated network scale is relatively small (typically 8 to 10 clients), leaving the scalability and communication/clustering behavior of SIMA in larger federated ecosystems unexplored.

PQ-LoRA requires an offline pre-alignment phase for matrices A and B using public proxy data (Dp) via MSE and CCA, which introduces a dependency on accessible, representative pre-training data before federated training begins.
SIMA requires every client to host and compute forward/backward passes on an auxiliary frozen model (Ws), which adds local storage and memory overhead despite the low gradient computation frequency.

Restricting trainable parameters to P and Q in the PQ-LoRA layers (freezing A and B) inherently restricts parameter expressiveness compared to standard LoRA, requiring careful tuning of the number of PQ-LoRA blocks versus conventional LoRA layers.

strengths: Addresses an important and realistic problem in federated learning: jointly tackling data heterogeneity (diverse multi-modal tasks under temporal distribution shifts) and model heterogeneity (models with different hidden dimensions and layer depths) for multi-modal LLMs.

Methodological novelty of PQ-LoRA: The introduction of dimension-invariant shareable modules P and Q sandwiched between frozen, aligned projection matrices A and B provides an elegant parameter-efficient mechanism to exchange weights across heterogeneous architectures without relying on costly federated distillation or logit transfer.

Well-motivated task similarity mechanism (SIMA): Utilizing exponential moving average (EMA) decayed gradients of the last layer from a small frozen anchor model efficiently tracks client task similarity under dynamic continuous data streams without heavy compute overhead.

Valuable benchmark contribution (DRAKE): DRAKE is an extensive, well-structured multi-modal federated benchmark comprising 40 distinct tasks across 19 datasets, supporting continual intra-client distribution shifts and evaluation on unseen tasks.

Extensive empirical validation: The paper includes comprehensive experiments across multiple foundation model families (LLaVA with LLaMA-3 and Qwen-2.5 variants), comparison with extensive state-of-the-art PFL baselines, evaluation of adaptation speed, and detailed ablations covering rank sizes, alignment choices, and component contributions.
weaknesses: Dependence on pre-alignment via public data: PQ-LoRA requires an offline alignment step on public data (using MSE and CCA) to align the frozen A and B matrices across heterogeneous client architectures before federated training begins. While practical using a subset of pretraining data, it introduces additional preprocessing complexity.

Constrained parameter capacity in PQ-LoRA layers: Because A and B remain frozen during local client training and only P and Q are updated, the expressiveness per adapted layer is bounded by r^2 parameters rather than r(d_I + d_O). As demonstrated in the ablation on N_B, placing PQ-LoRA on too many layers can trade off local personalization capacity.

Limited client scale: Due to the high compute costs of MLLMs, experimental evaluations are restricted to at most 10 clients. While reasonable for distributed foundation model research, behavior in larger federated federations with hundreds of heterogeneous clients remains unexplored.

strengths: Addresses an important and highly realistic problem: simultaneous data heterogeneity (diverse tasks and temporal distribution shifts) and model heterogeneity (varying hidden dimensions and depths) in multi-modal personalized federated learning (PFL).

Introduces DRAKE, a comprehensive and well-constructed multi-modal FL benchmark comprising 40 distinct tasks across 19 datasets, supporting multi-image reasoning and continual streaming data distributions.

The proposed PQ-LoRA offers a clean parameterization ($P \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times r}$, $Q \in \mathbb{R}^r$) enabling cross-architecture aggregation independent of model hidden dimensions, supported by formal proofs on zero aggregation error and representation span.

SIMA effectively tackles catastrophic forgetting and task interference in streaming federated scenarios using decayed gradient similarities computed via an exponential moving average on a lightweight pivot model.

Extensive experimental validation and ablations across multiple model families (LLaVA-Llama3 and LLaVA-Qwen2.5), both multi-modal and text-only LLM benchmarks (Fed-LLM, Fed-Aya), demonstrating consistent gains in both personalization and generalization.
weaknesses: Dependency on public data ($D_p$) for offline alignment: PQ-LoRA relies on an offline alignment phase of $A$ and $B$ matrices using public pre-training data via MSE and CCA before federated training starts. This requires the central coordinator to anticipate all candidate client model architectures beforehand.

Requirement of a shared auxiliary model ($W_s$): To compute gradient similarity in SIMA, all clients must store and run backward passes on a small frozen model $W_s$ (e.g., LLaVA-1B) in addition to their local models, which adds local storage and memory footprint on resource-constrained devices.

Uniform rank constraint: While PQ-LoRA handles depth and hidden-dimension heterogeneity, it strictly requires all clients to share the same low-rank dimension $r$ across all participating architectures to enable aggregation of $P$ and $Q$.

Small client scale: Experiments are restricted to at most 10 concurrent clients; while understandable given the high computational demands of fine-tuning multi-modal LLMs, evaluation at larger client counts would better reflect real-world federated deployment scenarios.

Marginal personalization improvement over Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on certain tasks (e.g., Client 2 and Client 3 in Table 3), showing that the benefit of federated collaboration remains uneven across clients.

strengths: Addresses an important and realistic problem: personalized federated learning with multi-modal large language models under simultaneous data heterogeneity (including temporal distribution shifts) and architecture/model heterogeneity.
Proposes DRAKE, a comprehensive, high-quality benchmark for multi-modal PFL featuring 40 tasks, temporal distribution shifts, and unseen tasks for out-of-distribution evaluation.

Methodologically sound design with PQ-LoRA, which decouples model-specific projection dimensions via frozen orthogonal matrices A and B and communicates only dimension-invariant (r x r) modules, effectively solving cross-architecture LoRA aggregation.

RELA provides a well-motivated relevance-guided aggregation strategy that uses decayed, sanitized gradients from a lightweight frozen reference model to mitigate task interference while preserving privacy and efficiency.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmarks (DRAKE, HFLB, Fed-Scope, Fed-Aya, Fed-LLM-Large up to 52 clients), cross-family models (Llama vs. Qwen), detailed efficiency analysis (FLOPs, memory, communication), and thorough ablations.
weaknesses: PQ-LoRA requires a one-time pre-federation alignment phase using public proxy data ($D_p$) to align heterogeneous model pairs before federated training begins, which introduces an extra operational requirement and may complicate setups where new model architectures join dynamically.

RELA requires each client to store and compute backpropagation on an auxiliary frozen model ($W_s$) to estimate task similarity; while the authors show this can be minimized with lightweight/quantized models, it remains an additional on-device overhead.

The performance improvement on client-specific personalization ('Self' accuracy) over local supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is relatively modest on simpler single-image tasks (e.g., Table 5), with the most pronounced benefits appearing primarily on complex multi-image tasks and cross-client generalization ('Others').

strengths: Addresses two critical and practical challenges in federated learning simultaneously: cross-architecture model heterogeneity (varying widths, depths, and model families) and temporal data/task heterogeneity in multimodal foundation models.

The proposed PQ-LoRA is an elegant, dimension-invariant parameter-efficient fine-tuning module (sharing only r x r and r-dimensional parameters) that avoids expensive logit extraction and distillation during federated communication while accommodating different model widths and depths.

RELA provides a well-motivated relevance-guided aggregation strategy that effectively tracks client task similarity under temporal distribution shifts using EMA-decayed, sanitized gradients from an auxiliary frozen model.

Introduction of DRAKE, a rich and realistic multimodal PFL benchmark spanning 40 distinct tasks from 19 datasets, incorporating multi-image reasoning, dynamic temporal distribution shifts, and explicit splits for evaluating unseen-task generalizability.

Extensive and thorough empirical evaluation across multimodal and text-only benchmarks, heterogeneous architectures (Llama and Qwen variants up to 8B), scaling up to 52 clients, supported by comprehensive ablation studies, communication/computation cost analyses, and fast-adaptation experiments.
weaknesses: Initial offline alignment of matrices A and B requires a small public dataset (Dp); while sensitivity analyses demonstrate robustness across domains and dataset sizes, this pre-federation alignment phase remains an added requirement.

Computing gradients on an auxiliary frozen model (Ws) introduces additional on-device memory and computational overhead, which may present practical constraints for very low-end edge clients, even with compression and periodic evaluation.

The theoretical contributions (Theorems 1 and 2) are relatively straightforward linear algebra observations (e.g., exact distributivity when outer matrices are frozen and identical), serving more as design justifications than deep theoretical insights.

On certain static tasks or simpler single-image VQA subsets, performance gains over standard local fine-tuning (SFT) and existing baselines are relatively modest (1–2%), with the largest benefits concentrated in complex multi-image tasks and rapid unseen adaptation.

strengths: Addresses a realistic, challenging, and highly practical setting: simultaneous data heterogeneity (multimodal tasks with temporal distribution shift) and model heterogeneity (varying model architectures, widths, depths, and model families) in personalized federated learning (PFL).

Introduction of the DRAKE benchmark, which spans 40 diverse multimodal tasks across 19 datasets, simulating dynamic data streams and explicitly evaluating out-of-distribution generalizability on unseen tasks.

Clever formulation of PQ-LoRA: by freezing the dimension-dependent projection matrices A and B and inserting shareable dimension-invariant modules P and Q, it enables cross-architecture weight aggregation without requiring uniform hidden dimensions or relying on expensive/domain-sensitive federated distillation.
RELA effectively mitigates task interference under streaming distribution shifts by tracking task relevance via decayed, sanitized gradients from an efficient frozen proxy model.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple multimodal and NLP benchmarks (including a large-scale setup with 52 clients), demonstrating consistent improvements over state-of-the-art PFL and federated distillation baselines in both personalization and generalization metrics.
weaknesses: The initial alignment of the PQ-LoRA matrices A and B requires an offline pre-alignment phase using a public proxy dataset Dp; although the authors show robustness across dataset sizes and domains, the requirement of suitable public data and offline coordination among model types remains a practical prerequisite.

RELA requires each client to perform forward/backward computation through an auxiliary frozen reference model Ws to compute task similarity gradients. Even though Ws can be quantized or downscaled, maintaining and running an auxiliary model imposes extra memory and compute overhead on edge devices with strict hardware constraints.

The privacy sanitization mechanism for transmitted gradients (EMA, Gaussian perturbation, and random subsampling) is heuristic and lacks a formal differential privacy (DP) guarantee or provable privacy budget bound.

In several static or less complex VQA tasks, local Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) already achieves very strong personalization performance, making the absolute gain of FedMosaic on 'Self' accuracy relatively incremental on those specific sub-tasks.
